note: Oct 26 2026 data fixes (stream data-fixes). Read by prefill/assemble.mjs after the expert review and before mods' approved suggestions (data/edits.json), so a rebuild keeps them. Every entry carries a 'why'. Licenses of added projects were read from each project's own LICENSE/COPYING file or its GitHub license field and run through the shared checker (checker/): see 'licenseSource' where the file was read by hand.

closedRemove.why: OpenVPN Community is open source (GPL-2.0), so it is not a closed app. Only OpenVPN Access Server, the paid admin product built on it, stays closed. Community is now listed as an alternative instead.
Duplicate spelling of Datadog in the same group.
Duplicate spelling of Power BI in the same group.
Apache Airflow is open source (Apache-2.0), so it is not a closed app. It is listed as an alternative instead.

closedRename.why: Odoo Community is open source (LGPL-3.0) and is listed as a project; only the paid Enterprise edition is closed. The same name was on both sides of the page.
The closed community-analytics service orbit.love shared its name with an unrelated open-source project, Orbit (a Jira-style task tool, listed under Task boards). Renamed so the two are not confused.

closedAdd.why: People search for the whole Office bundle; its page now shows the Documents, Spreadsheets and Slides alternatives together.
Same as Microsoft Office: the subscription name for the same bundle.
Google's bundle (Docs, Sheets, Slides); people search for the bundle name.

odoo.summary: Odoo is a suite of web-based business apps covering things like sales, accounting, inventory, websites and HR. The free Community edition is open source (LGPL-3.0); the paid Enterprise edition adds more features and is closed. It is for companies that want to run many business tasks in one connected system.
odoo.why: Odoo Community is LGPL-3.0 but Enterprise is proprietary, so it is shown as open core, which is the honest label.

cal-com.summary: Cal.diy is the free community edition of Cal.com. It lets you share a page where others pick a meeting time, and connects to your calendar so you are not double-booked. You run it on your own server, and its makers advise it for personal use only. Team and company features were removed from this edition.
cal-com.why: Checked against the repository's own README (Oct 26): calcom/cal.com now redirects to calcom/cal.diy (MIT, ~49k stars); the paid hosted Cal.com and its team features are separate. Wording made plain about what is missing.

mellisearch.name: Meilisearch
mellisearch.why: Misspelled: the project is Meilisearch (repo github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch, site meilisearch.com). Only the shown name is fixed; the internal id stays so existing links keep working.

semi.name: Weaviate
semi.why: Weaviate is the project (repo weaviate/weaviate); SeMI was its former company name. Only the shown name is fixed; the internal id stays so existing links keep working.

zinc-labs.name: ZincSearch
zinc-labs.summary: ZincSearch is a search engine that indexes text so you can find things quickly inside your own data. It is meant for developers and teams who want full text search without the complexity of Elasticsearch. Its README points people who want to search logs to OpenObserve, a separate product.
zinc-labs.why: The project is ZincSearch (repo zincsearch/zincsearch); Zinc Labs was the company. Its README says log search and cloud/high-availability belong to OpenObserve, a separate product, and zincsearch.com now forwards to openobserve.ai, so the docs site stays as the project link.

sonic.why: The listed website was a crates.io package page, not a project site. Sonic has no site of its own; the code link is shown instead.

pocket-casts.summary: Pocket Casts is a podcast app for finding, subscribing to and listening to shows on Android and iPhone. It is made for people who listen to podcasts on their phones.
pocket-casts.why: Website was the support forum; pocketcasts.com is the main site. The makers (Automattic) publish an iPhone app too (github.com/Automattic/pocket-casts-ios), so it is not Android-only.

quant-ux.why: Website was empty; the project runs a site at quant-ux.com (page title "Quant-UX - Prototype, Test and Learn").

comfyui.why: The README says ComfyUI is available on Windows, Linux and macOS; only Windows was listed.

jellyfin.why: jellyfin.org/downloads/clients lists official apps for Android, iOS and a desktop client, and the server also runs on Windows, Mac and Linux. The web player is built in.

calibre.why: calibre-ebook.com/download_linux exists: Calibre also runs on Linux, not just Windows and Mac.

whisper.why: Whisper is a Python package; its README gives install steps for Linux, macOS and Windows. It has no website of its own, so the code link is shown.

whisper-cpp.why: The README lists Apple Silicon (Mac) as first class, plus Linux, Windows, iOS and Android. It has no website of its own, so the code link is shown.

netdata.why: The README lists Linux, macOS, FreeBSD and Windows; only Windows was listed.

drone.name: Drone / Harness Open Source
drone.summary: Drone is a tool that builds, tests and deploys software automatically. Its makers' newer open source platform, Harness Open Source (the code linked here), adds code hosting, hosted development environments and artifact registries; the original Drone is kept on a separate branch of that code. It is for development teams who want to run these tools on their own machines or servers.
drone.why: The listed code is Harness Open Source, the successor platform; the Harness README ("Where is Drone?") says the original Drone is kept on the repo's "drone" branch and has its own site at drone.io. The name and text now say both.

quickwit.summary: Quickwit is a search engine for storing and searching large amounts of logs and traces, kept on cloud storage. It is aimed at engineers and operations teams who monitor software systems. Its team announced that Quickwit joined Datadog; the code remains open source.
quickwit.why: quickwit.io shows the banner "Quickwit joins Datadog!". The code is still open (Apache-2.0) and updated this week, so the listing stays; the summary now says so.

highlight.summary: Highlight is a monitoring platform that records user sessions, tracks errors and collects logs so developers can find out why bugs happen. It is aimed at software developers who run web apps. Its team has joined LaunchDarkly, and highlight.io now forwards to LaunchDarkly's site.
highlight.why: highlight.io now forwards to launchdarkly.com, and LaunchDarkly published "Welcome Highlight to LaunchDarkly". The code repo is still updated, so the listing stays; the summary now says so.

openblocks.summary: Openblocks is a tool for building internal business apps, such as dashboards and admin panels, by connecting to databases and APIs and arranging ready-made components on screen. It is aimed at software teams and companies that need custom tools for their staff or customers. The project has had no updates since October 2023; Lowcoder continues from it.
openblocks.why: The repo has had no changes since October 2023, and Lowcoder's README says it "continues from the abandoned Openblocks project".

heroic-games-launcher.summary: Heroic lets you sign in to your Epic, GOG and Amazon Games accounts and install and play the games you already own, on Windows, Mac and Linux. It also opens those stores inside the app; the games are sold by the stores, not by Heroic.
heroic-games-launcher.why: The README says "Access to Epic, GOG and Amazon Games stores directly from Heroic", so "sells none" misled. Heroic itself sells nothing; it opens the stores.

preset.name: Apache Superset
preset.why: The listed code and site are Apache Superset, the open project. Preset is a separate company that sells a hosted version of it, so the listing is named for the open project.

crater.summary: Crater is a free invoicing app you run yourself, with companion Android and iPhone apps, for making invoices and estimates and tracking expenses and payments. It is for individuals and small businesses that need to bill customers. It has had no updates since 2023, and its old website now shows a different product.
crater.why: Crater is a self-hosted web app (Laravel and Vue) with Android and iOS companion apps, not just phone apps (its README). craterapp.com now forwards to crater.financial, a different payments product, so the old site link is removed. The repo has had no changes since February 2023.

mlcraft.name: Synmetrix (formerly MLCraft)
mlcraft.why: The project was renamed Synmetrix; its README says "Synmetrix (prev. MLCraft)". Only the shown name is fixed; the internal id stays so existing links keep working.

postmarketos.name: Nura (formerly postmarketOS)
postmarketos.summary: Nura, formerly called postmarketOS, is a Linux-based operating system for phones, built to keep older devices useful for many years. It is for tinkerers: on most phones, calls, the camera or mobile data do not fully work yet.
postmarketos.why: postmarketos.org forwards to nura.eco, whose page says "Nura was formerly known as postmarketOS".

taiga.summary: Taiga is a free, open-source project management tool for agile teams, with boards for planning and tracking tasks and projects. You can run it yourself or use the hosted version at taiga.io. Its code is split across several repositories; the link goes to the main one.
taiga.why: The listed repo (kaleidos-ventures/taiga) is the "next iteration" rewrite, last changed in 2023. The live product at taiga.io runs from taigaio/taiga-back (changed this week, MPL-2.0) and taiga-front, so the code link, counts and activity now follow the live one. Hosted copies do not count for setup, so it is self-hosted.

kanboard.summary: Kanboard is project management software that uses Kanban boards to track tasks and their progress. It is for teams and individuals who want to organize work visually and host it themselves. Its makers describe it as in maintenance mode, which means no big new features are planned.
kanboard.why: Its README says "This application is in maintenance mode", but the repo is still updated, so it is not marked inactive.

openproject.why: openproject.org/collaboration-software-features says there is "a dedicated mobile app for iOS and Android".

etherpad.why: etherpad.org lists a desktop and mobile app for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS.

onlyoffice-docs.why: onlyoffice.com says free apps exist for iOS and Android.

localsend.why: localsend.org says it is available for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS.

plane.why: plane.so/mobile offers iOS and Android apps, and Plane Cloud is a hosted web version.

super-productivity.why: The README says it runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, iOS and in the browser.

comaps.why: The README says "Available for Android, iOS, MacOS, and Linux" and the site links the App Store.

home-assistant.why: home-assistant.io lists official Companion apps for iOS and Android.

spliit-app.why: spliit.app advertises "Spliit for iPhone", the public site works in a browser, and the README lists a Progressive Web App.

affine.why: affine.pro/download lists Android as well as iOS (Google Play and App Store).

gitlab-community-edition.why: Replaces the duplicate "Gitlab" listing (removed): github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq is itself described as "GitLab CE Mirror". Website was empty.

erp/odoo.note: Community edition is free and open; the paid Enterprise edition adds features
erp/odoo.why: Odoo is open core; see the erp note above.

shop/litekart.note: Storefront only; connects to a shop back end such as Shopify or Medusa
shop/litekart.why: Litekart is a storefront only; it connects to a separate shop back end (Shopify, Medusa, Saleor, WooCommerce...), per its README.

email/roundcube.note: Inbox screen only; connects to your existing email account
email/roundcube.why: Roundcube is an IMAP client (README): it needs a web server and any email account, not its own mail server.

addProjects.name: OpenBB
addProjects.summary: OpenBB is an open-source toolkit that pulls stock, economy and crypto data from many sources into one place, so you can chart and study it in code or spreadsheets. Its polished point-and-click workspace is a separate hosted product from the same company, not part of the open-source code.
addProjects.why: Asked for by Destin. LICENSE file says all files are Apache-2.0 (GitHub's own license field shows 'unclear', so the file was read by hand). The open part is the data toolkit; the Workspace app is hosted.

addProjects.name: OpenVPN
addProjects.summary: OpenVPN Community is the free, open-source VPN software behind many VPN services. You set up a server and connect your devices to it over an encrypted link. It works well but is set up by hand, without a friendly admin screen.
addProjects.why: COPYING file: GPL version 2 (with an exception for linking to OpenSSL). This is the Community edition, unlike the closed Access Server.

addProjects.name: ClickHouse
addProjects.summary: ClickHouse is a database built for asking questions about huge piles of data very quickly, such as website traffic or sales history. It runs on your own server and is often used in place of paid data warehouses.
addProjects.why: The most obvious open alternative to Snowflake was missing. GitHub license field: Apache-2.0.

addProjects.name: PostgreSQL
addProjects.summary: PostgreSQL is one of the world's most trusted databases: it stores business data in tables and answers questions about it. Many cloud database services are built on it. You can run it yourself on your own computer or server.
addProjects.why: The obvious open alternative to Amazon Aurora was missing from the map. The PostgreSQL License is OSI-approved (the checker accepts it); GitHub shows it as unclear only because it is a custom text.

addProjects.name: MariaDB
addProjects.summary: MariaDB is a popular free database for storing business and website data in tables. It started as a community branch of MySQL and works as a drop-in replacement for it. You run it on your own server.
addProjects.why: Common open alternative to Aurora-style SQL databases, missing from the map. GitHub license field: GPL-2.0.

addProjects.name: Apache Airflow
addProjects.summary: Apache Airflow lets technical teams write, schedule and watch jobs that move and prepare data, such as nightly imports. You describe each job in code and run Airflow on your own server.
addProjects.why: Airflow was wrongly listed as a closed app; it is open source, so it is added as a project instead.

addProjects.name: Mullvad VPN
addProjects.summary: Mullvad's VPN app hides your internet traffic from your network and shows a different location to websites. The app's code is open and has been independently audited, but the paid VPN service and its servers are run by Mullvad and are not open source.
addProjects.why: Consumer VPN alternatives. Honest limit: only the app is open, the service is paid.

addProjects.name: Proton VPN
addProjects.summary: Proton VPN hides your internet traffic and your location from websites. Its apps for phones and computers are open source and independently audited. The VPN service itself has a free plan and paid plans, and its servers are Proton's, not open source.
addProjects.why: Consumer VPN alternatives. Apps (several repos under github.com/ProtonVPN) are GPL-3.0; the service is not open. The Android app repo is linked.

addProjects.name: Outline VPN
addProjects.summary: Outline lets you set up your own private VPN on a server you rent, then share access with friends and family through a simple app. You control the server, but you only get the one location where you rented it.
addProjects.why: A fully open way to get a VPN for privacy; the catch is you run it yourself.

addProjects.name: diaspora*
addProjects.summary: diaspora* is a social network like Facebook that nobody owns. You join a community server (a pod) or run your own, share posts and photos with groups of friends you choose, and still talk to people on other pods.
addProjects.why: Facebook alternatives. GitHub license field: AGPL-3.0; last change July 2026.

addProjects.name: Pinry
addProjects.summary: Pinry lets you save pictures from around the web onto boards and browse them as a tiled wall, like Pinterest. You run it yourself, so your collection stays private unless you share it.
addProjects.why: Pinterest alternatives. GitHub license field: BSD-2-Clause.

addProjects.name: Linkwarden
addProjects.summary: Linkwarden saves web pages you want to keep, with a copy of each page, and sorts them into collections you can share. It is a good fit for building a private collection of things you found online.
addProjects.why: Pinterest alternatives (collecting links more than pictures). GitHub license field: AGPL-3.0.

addProjects.name: Karakeep
addProjects.summary: Karakeep is a place to save links, notes and images and find them again later, with automatic tags. It has apps for phones and a browser add-on. You run it on your own server.
addProjects.why: Pinterest alternatives (saving and tagging). GitHub license field: AGPL-3.0.

addProjects.name: LanguageTool
addProjects.summary: LanguageTool checks spelling, grammar and style in more than 30 languages. You can run the open-source checker on your own server so your writing never leaves your hands. The company's own apps and extensions add paid features.
addProjects.why: Grammarly alternatives. GitHub license field: LGPL-2.1.

addProjects.name: Harper
addProjects.summary: Harper is a fast grammar and spell checker that runs entirely on your own computer, so nothing you write is sent anywhere. It works in code editors and as a browser add-on, in English.
addProjects.why: Grammarly alternatives, private by design. GitHub license field: Apache-2.0.

addProjects.name: ClamAV
addProjects.summary: ClamAV is a free virus scanner that checks files and email for known malware. It is mostly used on servers and Linux computers. It has no polished windows or constant background protection on Windows and Mac.
addProjects.why: Antivirus alternatives. GitHub license field: GPL-2.0. OpenEDR was checked and left out: its license (Comodo Available Source License) is not open source.

addProjects.name: FreeCAD
addProjects.summary: FreeCAD is a free design program for making 3D models of real objects, such as parts, buildings and machines, and for creating drawings from them. It takes time to learn but is capable.
addProjects.why: CAD alternatives. GitHub license field: LGPL-2.1.

addProjects.name: LibreCAD
addProjects.summary: LibreCAD is a free program for flat, 2D technical drawings such as floor plans and part outlines. It opens and saves the common DXF drawing files. It does not do 3D.
addProjects.why: CAD alternatives. LICENSE file: GPL version 2.

addProjects.name: QCAD
addProjects.summary: QCAD is a program for 2D technical drawings that feels close to classic AutoCAD. The free Community Edition is open source; extra tools such as extra file formats come in a paid Professional edition.
addProjects.why: CAD alternatives. LICENSE.txt: source is GPL version 3; paid add-ons exist, so it is marked open core.

addProjects.name: OpenSCAD
addProjects.summary: OpenSCAD makes 3D models from a short written description instead of drawing with a mouse. It suits 3D printing and exact, repeatable parts.
addProjects.why: CAD alternatives. COPYING file: GPL version 2 with an exception for linking to the CGAL library.

addProjects.name: SolveSpace
addProjects.summary: SolveSpace is a small, fast program for designing 3D parts by sketching shapes and setting exact measurements. It is simpler than FreeCAD and good for mechanical parts.
addProjects.why: CAD alternatives. GitHub license field: GPL-3.0.

addProjects.name: Zotero
addProjects.summary: Zotero collects the articles, books and web pages you use for research, keeps your notes and PDFs together, and writes citations and bibliographies in Word or LibreOffice. It has a free plan with limited cloud storage.
addProjects.why: Reference manager alternatives to EndNote and Mendeley. COPYING file: GNU Affero GPL v3.

addProjects.name: JabRef
addProjects.summary: JabRef keeps a library of the papers and books you cite, in the BibTeX format used by LaTeX writers, and helps you find, sort and cite them. It runs on your computer.
addProjects.why: Reference manager alternatives. GitHub license field: MIT.

addProjects.name: Lutris
addProjects.summary: Lutris puts the games you own from different places in one library on Linux, and sets up what each needs to run, including many Windows games. It does not sell games.
addProjects.why: Game store alternatives. GitHub license field: GPL-3.0.

addProjects.name: Heroic Games Launcher
addProjects.summary: Heroic lets you sign in to your Epic, GOG and Amazon Games accounts and install and play the games you already own, on Windows, Mac and Linux. It does not sell games.
addProjects.why: Game store alternatives. GitHub license field: GPL-3.0.

addProjects.name: Playnite
addProjects.summary: Playnite gathers your PC games from Steam, Epic, GOG and others into one library with one search. It launches and tracks them, but does not sell games.
addProjects.why: Game store alternatives. GitHub license field: MIT.

addProjects.name: itch app
addProjects.summary: The itch app is the free desktop app for itch.io, a store for independent games. It downloads and updates the games you got there. The itch.io store itself is a service run by itch, not open source.
addProjects.why: Game store alternatives. GitHub license field: MIT. Only the app is open.
